lesson.text: Quick memory: in grade 6, what are serifs? (Small strokes at the ends of letters, as on Trajan's Column.) Today: designing a logo and a poster.
Graphic design puts words and pictures together to send a message clearly: posters, logos, signs, book covers, the buttons in this game. Good design is seen, read and understood quickly.
A logo is a small symbol for a club or a group. A good logo is simple, easy to remember, clear when tiny and big, and still works in one colour.
Test a logo: shrink it. Thin lines and small words turn to a smudge, so a busy logo fails, while a simple shape stays clear. Then try it in black only, and in white on a dark background.
A poster needs a hierarchy: the most important thing biggest (the headline), then the picture, then the details (what, when, where). The eye reads them in that order.
Layout: line things up on a grid, keep a margin round the edge, and leave white space. Empty space is not wasted: it lets each part breathe. Use one or two typefaces at most.
Worked example: this crowded poster uses seven sizes, six colours and no space, so nothing stands out. The clear poster has one big headline, one picture and short details on a grid.
Try it in the world: design a poster for a made-up event with one headline, one picture and three lines of details. Add a simple logo that works tiny. Next: designing buildings.

exercises.prompt: What should be biggest on a poster?
exercises.hint: What should the eye see first?
exercises.explain: The headline: the most important thing is biggest.

exercises.prompt: Empty space on a poster is wasted space.
exercises.hint: What does white space do for the other parts?
exercises.explain: False: white space lets each part breathe and stand out.

exercises.hint: Imagine it on a tiny badge.
choices: simple and clear even when tiny
exercises.explain: Simple shapes stay clear at any size and in one colour.

exercises.prompt: Label the parts of this poster.
exercises.hint: Biggest words at the top, the picture in the middle, small words below.
exercises.explain: The headline at the top, the image, the details below, and the white space beside them.

exercises.prompt: Which poster is easier to read?
exercises.hint: Which one shows you where to look first?
exercises.explain: The clear one: one big headline, one picture, short details and plenty of space.

exercises.prompt: Why does the busy logo fail when it is small?
exercises.hint: Look at the tiny copy of each.
choices: its thin lines and words become a smudge
exercises.explain: Shrunk, the thin lines and tiny words blur together; the simple owl stays clear.

exercises.prompt: Match each design word to its meaning.
exercises.hint: Think of how a clear poster is built.
exercises.explain: Hierarchy: order of importance; margin: edge space; grid: alignment lines; typeface: letter design.

exercises.prompt: How many typefaces should a clear poster use?
exercises.hint: Too many kinds of letter look messy.
choices: a new one for every line
exercises.explain: One or two: one for the headline and one for the rest.

exercises.prompt: A good logo still works in one colour.
exercises.hint: Think of a logo printed in black on a letter.
exercises.explain: True: a strong logo works in one colour, and reversed.

exercises.prompt: Put the parts in the order the eye should read them.
exercises.explain: Headline, then picture, then details, and the small logo last.

exercises.prompt: Which poster is laid out symmetrically, down the middle?
exercises.hint: Look for everything centred on one line down the middle.
exercises.explain: The centred poster: its headline, picture and details all sit on the middle line.

exercises.prompt: The details are too small to read from across a room. What should change?
exercises.hint: Keep the hierarchy but make everything readable.
choices: make them bigger, and keep the headline biggest
exercises.explain: Make the details bigger while the headline stays the biggest thing.

exercises.prompt: Which is the best logo for a castle-building club?
exercises.hint: Which would still work on a tiny badge in one colour?
choices: a photo of a real castle
the full name in tiny letters
exercises.explain: A simple tower shape: bold, memorable and clear at any size.

exercises.prompt: Why line things up on a grid?
exercises.hint: Compare the clear poster with the crowded one.
choices: the page looks tidy and is easier to read
it makes everything the same size
exercises.explain: Things lined up look organised, so the eye moves easily from part to part.

exercises.prompt: Every word on a poster should be the same size so nothing is missed.
exercises.hint: What happens when everything shouts at once?
exercises.explain: False: if everything is the same size, nothing stands out. Hierarchy tells the eye where to start.

exercises.prompt: Which colour makes a headline stand out on a pale blue poster?
exercises.hint: Think of contrast in colour and in lightness.
exercises.explain: Dark orange contrasts in colour (orange is opposite blue) and in lightness.

exercises.prompt: Sort the logo ideas: will it still work when tiny?
exercises.hint: Shrink each one in your mind to the size of a fingernail.
exercises.explain: Bold, simple shapes stay clear: a tower, an owl outline, one big letter. Long sentences, detailed photos and thin lines blur into a smudge.

exercises.prompt: Order the steps to design a clear poster.
items: Check it from across a room.
exercises.hint: Follow the hierarchy, most important first, then test it.
exercises.explain: Write the big headline, choose one strong picture, add the short details on a grid, then check it from across a room: can you read it at a glance?

exercises.prompt: Sort the poster choices: clearer, or more cluttered?
exercises.hint: Clear design keeps things few, lined up and with room to breathe.
exercises.explain: Clearer: one or two typefaces, a margin, white space between the parts. More cluttered: seven text sizes, six bright colours and text touching the edges, so nothing stands out.
